summary: Specifies version 7 of the Bundle Protocol for delay-tolerant networking, adapted from the experimental protocol in RFC 5050. It is designed for networks where connections can be long delayed or intermittent, such as in space. Data travels as bundles that are stored and forwarded when links become available. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Messages wait at each stop until the next road opens, like passing a parcel across a place with no steady roads.

questions: what is a bundle in dtn
how does bpv7 differ from rfc 5050
subtitle: A store-and-forward protocol that moves data across networks where links are slow, intermittent or absent.

tldr.problem: Ordinary Internet protocols assume a connected path with short delays. In stressed networks with intermittent connectivity, large or variable delays and high bit error rates, that assumption fails.
tldr.mechanism: The Bundle Protocol sends self-contained units called bundles, encoded in CBOR. Each node stores a bundle, carries it, and forwards it when a link next becomes available, so the sender and receiver need not be connected at the same time.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9171 standardizes version 7 of the protocol, adapted from the experimental RFC 5050. It is not interoperable with RFC 5050 and has since been updated by RFC 9713 and RFC 9758.

today: RFC 9171 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022. It is updated by RFC 9713 and RFC 9758, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why Bundles Exist
sections.content:
RFC 9171 specifies Bundle Protocol version 7 (BPv7) for Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN). DTN is a network architecture for stressed environments: intermittent connectivity, large or variable delays and high bit error rates. The protocol is adapted from the experimental Bundle Protocol of RFC 5050, using lessons from implementations in several programming languages.

BP can be seen as sitting at the application layer of a number of constituent networks, forming a store-carry-forward overlay network. Its key capabilities include using physical motility to move data, moving responsibility for error control from one node to another, coping with cases where sender and receiver are never in the network at the same time, and late binding of endpoint identifiers to underlying network addresses.

The RFC leaves several things out: the work done inside convergence-layer adapters, route computation, how routing tables are filled, how bundles are secured en route, and how nodes are managed. It also warns that BPv7 implementations will not interoperate with RFC 5050 implementations.
sections.eli5: Some places, like deep space, have no steady connection. Instead of waiting for one, the data hops from stop to stop and rests at each stop until the next hop is ready.

sections.title: Nodes, Endpoints and Services
sections.content:
The unit of data is a bundle: a sequence of two or more blocks that carries an application data unit (ADU) together with the metadata needed to make it usable on arrival. Bundling the metadata matters because negotiating parameters may be impractical in a delay-tolerant network.

A bundle node has three conceptual parts: a Bundle Protocol Agent (BPA) that executes the protocol, zero or more convergence-layer adapters (CLAs) that send and receive bundles over an underlying network, and an application agent (AA). The AA has an administrative element, which handles records such as status reports, and an application-specific element.

Bundles are addressed to endpoints, which are sets of zero or more nodes sharing an endpoint ID. A singleton endpoint has exactly one member. Every node is permanently registered in its own administrative endpoint, and that endpoint's ID serves as the node ID. A registration is local state describing a node's membership in an endpoint and is either Active or Passive.

The BPA offers its application agent services to start and end registrations, switch them between Active and Passive, transmit a bundle, cancel a transmission, poll a Passive registration and deliver a received bundle. The protocol itself does not ensure delivery; the RFC says end-to-end assurance needs extensions or application-layer mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Each stop on the route has a mail clerk, a set of trucks for different roads, and the people who send and read the mail. Addresses can name one stop or a whole group of stops.

sections.title: The Bundle Format
sections.content:
Bundles are encoded in CBOR (RFC 8949), using the core deterministic encoding so that a block's canonical form is the same everywhere. That makes cryptographic verification possible. A bundle is a CBOR indefinite-length array of at least two blocks: exactly one primary block first, then one or more canonical blocks, ending with exactly one payload block and a CBOR break code.

The primary block is immutable. It is an array of 8, 9, 10 or 11 elements depending on whether the bundle is a fragment and whether the block has a CRC. Its fields, in order, are version, bundle processing control flags, CRC type, destination EID, source node ID, report-to EID, creation timestamp, lifetime, then fragment offset and total ADU length for fragments only, and finally the CRC if present.

Every other block is a canonical block with 5 or 6 elements: block type code, block number, block processing control flags, CRC type, block-type-specific data and an optional CRC. The payload block has type code 1 and block number 1. Block type codes 192 through 255 are available for private or experimental use.

A CRC type of 0 means no CRC, 1 means an X-25 CRC-16 and 2 means a CRC32C. Stronger integrity protection is left to Block Integrity Blocks from BPSec (RFC 9172).
sections.eli5: A bundle is a parcel with an address label on the outside and one or more compartments inside. The last compartment always holds the actual message.

sections.title: Identifiers, Time and Flags
sections.content:
Endpoint IDs are URIs, encoded on the wire as a two-item CBOR array: a numeric scheme code and the scheme-specific part. Two schemes are defined here. The dtn scheme uses character strings, with dtn:none naming the null endpoint, which never has members. In the ipn scheme an ID is a node number and a service number, such as ipn:node.service, and all such endpoints are singletons. A zero demux or a zero service number may identify a node's administrative endpoint.

DTN time is an unsigned integer count of milliseconds since 2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, ignoring leap seconds; zero means the time is unknown. A bundle's creation timestamp pairs the creation time with a sequence number kept by the source node. Nodes without accurate clocks are advised to set creation time to zero and never reset the counter.

Bundle processing control flags are a bit field in the primary block. They mark a fragment, an administrative record, a do-not-fragment request, an application acknowledgement request, a status time request, and requests for reception, forwarding, delivery and deletion status reports. Block processing control flags tell a node what to do when it cannot process a block: replicate it in every fragment, send a status report, delete the bundle, or discard the block. Unrecognized flags MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: Addresses are like street names or house numbers. The clock starts counting from the year 2000, and little checkboxes on the label say things like "do not split this parcel" or "tell me when it arrives".

sections.title: How Nodes Process Bundles
sections.content:
A node tracks each bundle with retention constraints such as Dispatch pending, Forward pending and Reassembly pending. A bundle cannot be discarded while it has any constraint.

On reception, the node checks the CRC of each block. A malformed block or CRC mismatch means the bundle MUST be deleted for the reason Block unintelligible. For extension blocks the node cannot process, the block's own flags decide whether to send a status report, delete the bundle or discard the block. Then the bundle is dispatched: if the node is a member of the destination endpoint, the bundle is delivered locally.

On forwarding, the BPA selects next nodes and the CLAs to reach them. If it cannot, forwarding is contraindicated and the BPA decides whether to declare failure, in which case it may send the bundle back to the previous node or delete it. Otherwise it waits and tries again later. A forwarding node adjusts the Previous Node and Bundle Age blocks before sending.

A bundle expires when its age exceeds its lifetime and the BPA MUST then delete it. A BPA MAY impose a shorter temporary lifetime override. Fragmentation replaces a bundle with two bundles carrying the first N and last M-N payload bytes; the destination reassembles the original ADU from fragments sharing a source node ID and creation timestamp.
sections.eli5: Each stop checks that the parcel is not damaged, then either hands it to the person it is for or waits for a road to the next stop. If the parcel is too old, it is thrown away. A big parcel can be split into smaller ones and put back together at the end.

sections.title: Extension Blocks and Status Reports
sections.content:
Three extension blocks are defined, and every implementation MUST be able to recognize, parse and act on them, though not necessarily produce them.

  • The Previous Node Block (type 6) names the node that forwarded the bundle to the current node.
  • The Bundle Age Block (type 7) holds the age in milliseconds, for nodes without accurate clocks. If creation time is zero, the bundle MUST carry exactly one.
  • The Hop Count Block (type 10) holds a hop limit, which MUST be in the range 1 through 255, and a hop count. When the count exceeds the limit, the bundle SHOULD be deleted with the reason Hop limit exceeded.

Bundle status reports are the one administrative record type defined, with record type code 1. They report whether a node received, forwarded, delivered or deleted a bundle, with an optional time, plus a reason code. Table 1 of the RFC lists reason codes 0 through 11, including Lifetime expired (1), Depleted storage (4), No known route to destination from here (6), Hop limit exceeded (9) and Block unsupported (11).

One requester can trigger many reports: the RFC notes that a single bundle might generate (1 + (2*(N-1))) status report bundles over a path of N nodes. For that reason, status report generation MUST be disabled by default.
sections.eli5: Extra sticky notes can be added to a parcel: who handed it over, how long it has been travelling, and how many stops it has made. Stops can also send postcards saying "the parcel arrived here", but these are off unless someone turns them on.

sections.title: Security and the Convergence Layer
sections.content:
BP security services are provided by Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec, RFC 9172) rather than any other mechanism with the same scope. A BPA that sources, verifies or accepts a bundle MUST implement BPSec support, though using it on any single bundle is optional. BPSec adds integrity blocks (BIBs) and confidentiality blocks (BCBs) as extension blocks, so protection applies while a bundle waits at a node as well as in transit. Convergence-layer protocols that give authenticity and confidentiality between neighbors SHOULD be used where available.

The RFC names two denial-of-service concerns: malicious status report requests, which is why they are disabled by default, and many fragments with long lifetimes occupying storage while awaiting reassembly. Lifetime overrides are the suggested defense. It also warns that nodes unaware their clocks are inaccurate may behave unexpectedly.

The convergence layer must supply three services to the BPA: send a bundle to a reachable node, report the outcome, and deliver a received bundle. Because long round-trip times make end-to-end reactive congestion control unworkable, convergence-layer protocols MUST provide rate limiting or congestion control. The TCP convergence-layer adapter (RFC 9174) MUST be implemented when bundles must be forwarded over the Internet.
sections.eli5: Locks and seals on the parcel come from a separate rulebook. Each road between stops also has to make sure it does not get jammed with too many parcels.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 5050
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the significant changes from RFC 5050:

  • Transmission is distinguished from forwarding.
  • Custody transfer moves to a separate bundle-in-bundle encapsulation specification.
  • A node ID becomes a distinct concept from an endpoint ID, with the same syntax.
  • The primary block is restructured and made immutable, with an optional CRC; non-primary blocks also gain optional CRCs.
  • Canonical blocks gain a block number, to support BPSec.
  • The Bundle Age, Previous Node and Hop Count extension blocks are defined.
  • Quality of Service markings are removed.
  • Self-Delimiting Numeric Values give way to CBOR encoding.
  • Lifetime overrides are added, and time values are stated in milliseconds, not seconds.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what changed since the first version: a tidier label, a built-in damage check, and a new way of writing numbers.
